```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(rcupp)
```

`rcupp` ships a small, dependency-free set of diagnostic functions for
profiling memory use and method run time. They are built for **diagnosis**,
not for benchmark headlines: the numbers describe what happened in one run on
your machine, with all of its overhead and noise. This vignette explains the
four things they measure, how to read them, and where the honest limits are.
No GPU is required to run it; on the CPU fallback the device fields are `NA`.

## Which backend is linked

Every diagnostic reports the linked backend. When `rcupp` is built without the
CUDA toolkit there is no device to measure, so the device-derived fields are
`NA_real_`; the timing and R-heap fields still work and no call errors.

```{r backend}
cuda_available()
```

## GPU device memory

`rcupp_device_memory()` takes a whole-device snapshot through
`cudaMemGetInfo()`. It reports free, total, and used memory in bytes and MiB,
plus `available`, `cuda`, and `backend` flags.

```{r device-memory}
mem <- rcupp_device_memory()
mem$backend
mem$available
mem$free_mb
```

`used` is `total - free` for the **whole device**, not a byte count of any
single object: other processes and rcupp's own caching allocator also move it.
On the CPU fallback `available` is `FALSE` and the numeric fields are
`NA_real_`. A before/after difference is available inside `rcupp_profile()`.

## Method timing

`rcupp_bench()` evaluates an expression several times and reports the spread
of wall-clock and device time. Prefer it over a single reading: on WSL and
under host load, cold GPU calls and clock ramp make one number unreliable.

```{r bench}
b <- rcupp_bench(1 + 1, reps = 5)
b$wall_ms_median
b$wall_ms_min
b$wall_ms_max
```

There is no absolute threshold implied by these numbers. Use the distribution
to see how noisy a given workload is, not to claim a speedup.

## Device time versus host overhead

`rcupp_tic()` and `rcupp_toc()` bracket a region with a pair of CUDA events on
the default stream, the stream every rcupp operator uses. `rcupp_toc()`
returns device-side elapsed milliseconds, or `NA_real_` when CUDA is absent.

We use a small data set so the example stays cheap on every backend.

```{r data}
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(60 * 5), 60, 5)
y <- rnorm(60)
```

```{r tic-toc}
rcupp_tic()
invisible(lasso_fista(X, y, 0.1))
rcupp_toc()
```

`rcupp_profile()` combines that device timer with a host wall clock
(`proc.time()`), R heap accounting (`gc()`), and a before/after device-memory
delta in one call. The expression is evaluated in the calling frame and its
value is kept in `$result`, so the work is not wasted.

```{r profile}
p <- rcupp_profile(lasso_fista(X, y, 0.1))
p$wall_ms
p$device_ms
p$host_overhead_ms
```

`device_ms` is elapsed time on the default stream: kernels plus synchronous
host-device transfers. `host_overhead_ms` is the remainder of wall time (R
overhead, handle and `cudaMalloc` setup, just-in-time compilation, and clock
ramp). This is a **device-versus-wall split, not per-kernel attribution**.
Telling which individual kernel cost what needs external tooling such as
Nsight Systems or NVTX markers; rcupp does not instrument the operator hot
path.

On WSL/CUDA each tiny operator call carries a few milliseconds of fixed
overhead and GPU clocks ramp lazily, so a single `device_ms` is dominated by
that overhead. Read it as a diagnostic hint, and use `rcupp_bench()` to see the
distribution.

## R heap memory

`rcupp_memory_report()` is a standalone snapshot of R's heap via `gc()`, with
a device snapshot for context. `r_cells_used` and `r_cells_max_used` are
retained heap cells.

```{r memory-report}
r <- rcupp_memory_report()
r$r_cells_used
r$r_cells_max_used
```

Inside `rcupp_profile()`, `r_cells_net_delta` is the net change in retained
heap cells and `r_cells_peak` is the peak after `gc(reset = TRUE)`. Both are
**retained-heap figures, not cumulative bytes allocated**; use `Rprofmem()` for
a full allocation trace. The `device_*_delta_bytes` fields are whole-device
`cudaMemGetInfo()` differences and are approximate, because transient buffers
are freed before a call returns.

## Reading the numbers honestly

* These are **diagnostic snapshots**, not benchmarks. They do not isolate GPU
  acceleration from compilation, host-device transfers, or R-to-C++ boundary
  cost.
* On the CPU fallback every device-derived field is `NA_real_`, by design.
* A single measurement is noisy. Use `rcupp_bench()` and report the spread.
* `device_ms` is a default-stream total, not a per-kernel breakdown.

For real per-kernel attribution, reach for external profilers; for honest
whole-method comparisons, keep the baseline and conditions explicit.
